section.title: How to read this appendix
section.para: changes from the first edition This appendix collects, in one place, every rule of Lojban that this edition teaches differently from the first edition. The first edition appeared in 1997, and its revisions up to version 1.1 corrected it. Those corrections were errata, not rule changes. Where this book teaches a changed rule, a status note marks it, and this appendix is the index of those notes.

tells the story of the governance behind these changes. In brief, a language-definition committee (the BPFK) and its parent organization (the LLG) adopted a small number of deliberate amendments between 2004 and 2016. Both bodies are now effectively inactive. The last recorded meeting of the LLG began in 2022 and ended in 2023. So the official language is frozen as amended.
Every entry below carries one of these authority labels:

listitem.para: An LLG vote adopted the rule. Only the reform of the article system has this status.
A recorded BPFK vote adopted the rule, and the LLG never separately ratified it.
The committee fixed the rule in its checkpoint process of 2004–2005. The frozen snapshot texts of those dates are the authoritative statements.

No official body voted on the rule. The entry states its class of evidence. The class is a working document of the definition effort, implementation by the current tools that this edition surveyed, attested usage, or a combination. No single class proves consensus by itself.
This edition adopts a convention where the official texts are silent or unsettled. The entry always says so.

section.para: In 2007, the LLG adopted the article reform as its working baseline. It made one promise at that time, and that promise extends in spirit to everything here. Text written to the rules of the first edition is not incorrect. It is older Lojban. This appendix exists so that readers can move between the two.

erratacorrections since the first edition Apart from the rule changes below, the successive revisions corrected genuine errors in the Lojban of the first edition. These were wrong words in printed examples. For example, one example had a le'u where the quotation opener lo'u belonged. Others had a le ka for a le du'u, or a mis-split na'e ke. Those were mistakes when printed, and this edition fixes them. They are not changes to the language, and this appendix does not list them.

One more change is to the book, not to the language. The first edition printed the machine-oriented grammar (YACC) in full. This edition prints only the human-oriented EBNF grammar (see ), and the machine grammars are still available as electronic supplements. The YACC listing is gone because of an informal majority at the 2014 annual meeting of the LLG. That was a decision about what to print, not about the grammar itself.

The official definition of Lojban syntax is still the EBNF/YACC grammar of the third baseline. The camxes PEG grammars that current software uses are the de facto standard, and nobody ever ratified them.

section.title: The article system (xorlo)
section.para:
xorlosummary of changes
This change is ratified. The BPFK first checkpointed it in 2004, the LLG adopted it as the working baseline in 2007, and an LLG vote ratified it in 2020. The vote made one revision of the committee's gadri page the official description: MediaWiki revision 123823 (3 April 2020). The vote added two expressly stated corrections: a typo, mokla for moklu, and a repaired final clause in the unicorn example of the page.

This is the largest change in the book.
teaches it, and it is fundamental to . The first edition gave every description hidden default quantifiers: lo broda meant su'o lo ro broda, and le broda meant ro le su'o broda. The reform abolishes all default quantifiers. An unquantified description is a constant, and it refers to whatever things the context supplies. (Formally, lo broda is zo'e noi ke'a broda.)
The consequences run through the whole book:

listitem.para: lo is the everyday default article. It refers to one or more things that really fit its description, with no implicit quantifier or count machinery.
An outer quantifier, when actually said, selects distributively from the referents of a description.
An inner quantifier states the count of the referents.
PA broda means PA da poi broda, and it is no longer an abbreviation of PA lo broda.
Groups (gunma), with collective satisfaction and properties of their own, replace the old mass doctrine, in which a mass has the properties of its components.

The gloss of me is sharper: is/are among the referents of, not is one of. This is a clarification from a working document, and no official body separately voted on it. But the ratified expansions rely on it.
A number directly after la is part of the name, not an inner quantifier.

section.para:
Some lessons of the first edition about attachment to descriptors derived from the abolished defaults.
and
derive them again.

implicit quantifiersfirst-edition table of
To help you read older text, here is the abolished machinery in full. The first edition held that every sumti carried one or two implicit quantifiers. These applied automatically whenever no explicit quantifiers appeared. For the descriptors, they were these:

tr.td: all of the at-least-one described as
at least one of all of those which really are
some part of the mass of the at-least-one described as
some part of the mass of all those that really are
some part of the mass of the at-least-one named
the whole of the set of the at-least-one described as
the whole of the set of all those that really are
the whole of the set of the at-least-one named

section.para: Beyond the descriptors, personal pro-sumti carried an implicit ro, or pisu'o when read as masses. The first edition said that the composite pro-sumti like mi'o represent masses, equal to the joi forms. Quotations carried an implicit su'o, and other kinds of sumti had defaults too.

The consequences ran deep. Because lo broda contained a real at least one, every bare description was a quantified claim, subject to the scope rules of . An inner quantifier on lo counted everything in existence that fits the description. So the first edition warned readers away from lo ci gerku, because it claims that only three dogs exist.

The first edition also drew a sharp contrast in the placement of incidental clauses. In lo prenu ku noi blabi, the clause applied after the outer su'o selected. But lo prenu noi blabi put the clause inside the description. There the hidden inner ro made it a claim that all persons whatsoever are white. And the lessons of the first edition about definite and indefinite descriptions were largely lessons about which defaults you got.
None of this survives. An unquantified description is a constant, and the only quantifiers in a bridi are the ones that somebody said.

massesfirst-edition doctrine
The mass of the first edition was also a stranger thing than the group of today. The first edition said that a mass inherits the properties of each of its components, where they are relevant to it. It also said that a mass has properties of its own. So a mass of people with fair-skinned and dark-skinned members had fair skin and dark skin. (But the mass was not of molecular size merely because the molecules of its people are.) As a result, ordinary logical reasoning did not apply to statements about masses.

A group (gunma) has whatever properties it has, collectively satisfied or not, and logic applies as usual. The first edition also used loi for generic statements about kinds. It read loi cinfo cu xabju le fi'ortu'a, Lions dwell in Africa, as some part of the mass of all lions dwells in Africa. That is true because some lions do, and for the same reason it is too weak to say that lions generally do. In current Lojban, plain lo cinfo cu xabju lo fi'ortu'a says it, because lo is fully generic.

listitem.para: dotsidechange summary This change is committee-approved: a recorded BPFK vote adopted it on 8 August 2015, with seven votes in favor and one abstention. The LLG never separately ratified it. Every cmevla has a dot at the start and at the end. The first edition's ban on la, lai, la'i, and doi inside cmevla no longer applies. This edition uses the rule throughout.

consonant-glide-vowel banchange summary This change is committee-approved and de facto. The committee approved it on 27 December 2014, in a vote from the transition period before its reauthorization in 2015. The surveyed grammars of word forms implement it. No word can contain a consonant directly followed by a glide. So this edition spells the first edition's kuarka and .niuport. as ku'arka and .ni'uport. (see
and ).

diphthongschange summary This change is de facto: it comes from a working document of the definition effort, and the surveyed parsers implement it. Only ai, ei, oi, and au are diphthongs. The first edition had ten other diphthongs, and it permitted them only in attitudinal indicators and in Lojbanized names and borrowings. They are now glide-initial syllables, permitted at the start of a word or after a vowel. The two diphthongs that the first edition allowed only in names, iy and uy, are also syllables with a glide and then y.

The same grammar makes word resolution deterministic. At each point the first matching rule wins, so a string of Lojban text breaks into words in exactly one way. The grammar also extends the space of permitted experimental cmavo shapes, and it admits digits inside cmevla. For each word class, it states rules for consonantal syllables and for stress. The appendices of this edition print the full grammar.

fu'ivlacluster position, change summary This change is de facto: it comes from a working document of the definition effort, and the surveyed parsers implement it. The consonant cluster of a fu'ivla no longer has to fall within the first five letters of the word. The first edition required that of every brivla. Gismu and classical lujvo satisfy it by construction, and a lujvo that begins with a fu'ivla rafsi can inherit the cluster position of the fu'ivla. For fu'ivla, the working grammar keeps only the structural requirement: the word must resolve as a single brivla. So a word like ro'i'inre'o (with its cluster at the fifth and sixth letters) is now a valid fu'ivla (see ).

rafsiextended, change summary This change is de facto: it comes from a working document of the definition effort, and the surveyed parsers implement it. Every fu'ivla has combining forms, and in final position it stays unchanged. (A fu'ivla that begins with a vowel also takes a leading apostrophe when anything attaches before it.) Elsewhere, it takes 'y, or, when no collision arises, its final vowel changes to y. In every case, the whole result must still break apart into the intended words.
The first edition allowed fu'ivla only in zei compounds. In place of combining forms, it printed a proposal for cultural fu'ivla that no official body ever adopted (see ).

hyphenschange summary The norm is editorial, and the acceptance is de facto: the surveyed parsers implement it. As the norm for writers, this edition keeps the classical, minimal rules for hyphen placement. The working grammar deliberately also accepts unneeded hyphens. In 2019, an attempt to make that official for the previous revision of the book was vetoed.

commachange summary This change is editorial, and it follows the working grammar. The comma is only an aid to pronunciation. It cannot make an otherwise invalid letter sequence valid. This reverses several lessons of the first edition that depended on it.

The first edition allowed a comma to sound like an apostrophe, [h]. But it also said that commas never distinguish words. No official decision ever settled that conflict. The working grammar of word forms resolves it: it ignores commas entirely.

The first edition also allowed three other uses of the comma. It let a comma force a division between syllables, or another grouping of syllables. It let names contain commas with a sound, as in .i,ai,i,ai,on.. And it let a comma separate syllables in a borrowing, to permit a sequence of vowels. For example, bang,r,kore,a is now bangrkore'a, with an apostrophe.
All of these devices are gone: spell the pronunciation that you want (see ).

tagsbinding change summary This change is committee-approved: seven of eight members voted for it on 15 March 2016, and the LLG never separately ratified it. A tense or modal tag directly before a selbri binds to that selbri exactly as cu does. But an explicit ku that ends the tag construct first breaks the binding. So lo nu broda ba brode is a complete bridi. The grammar of the first edition absorbed such tags into the preceding construct. See , and the guidance on elision in .

magic wordschange summary The rules for each word are checkpointed (2005), and the synthesis is editorial. Each quoting and binding word received a fixed left-to-right rule for conflicts. These rules replace the inconsistent pairwise list of the first edition. The committee's decision on quotations covers zo, zoi, la'o, and lo'u. Its decision on connectives covers zei. A definition with a list of exceptions covers bu.

The y and fa'o rules have their own checkpointed definitions. The capture exceptions of fa'o name zo, lo'u…le'u, service as a zoi delimiter, and a preceding zei. Capture inside the quoted text of a zoi follows from the zoi rule itself. This edition presents all of this under one uniform principle. It flags the two contested corners: whether bu can bind the BAhE words, and whether le'u bu is a letteral.

The zo le'u loophole of the first edition is gone. A quotation now erases as a single unit, so zo si si leaves nothing. The first edition counted the pieces of a quotation separately, so it took three si words to repair a stray zo. The first edition also noted that its own machine parser did not implement si erasure at all. The parsers that this edition surveyed do implement it.

No official body ever voted on erasure. The boundary rules that this edition teaches come from the community's later proposal on erasure. The rule for si, as taught, is de facto: the surveyed parsers all implement it the same way. The rule for su is de facto, but the implementations are uneven. The surveyed parsers disagree on whether the paragraph boundary itself survives.

The word sa remains unsettled. When the committee froze the rest of the word-level machinery, it deliberately left the precise rule for sa undecided. A later proposal (erase back to the last word of the same selma'o) never gained standing, and parsers implement different approximations. See .

fi'orestriction changes summary This change is de facto: the surveyed parsers implement it. Two parser restrictions of the first edition on fi'o modals no longer apply: modal connectives and sticky modals now parse. Direct negation still does not parse. See .

gekstags before, change summary This change is de facto: the surveyed parsers implement it, and no official body voted on it. A tense or modal tag can now stand directly before a forethought connective, as in pu ge broda gi brode. The grammar reads it as a tag on the whole connected bridi. The grammar of the first edition rejected this outright, unless ke followed the tag. But the first edition's own prose used the bare form (see ).

section.title: Tenses
section.para: ZAhOchange summary This change is checkpointed (24 May 2004). An event contour used as a sumtcita now has the reverse reading from the first edition. In broda ba'o lo nu brode, the main bridi carries the contour, at the time of the tagged event. This is the same as ba'o broda ca lo nu brode.

The first edition read it the other way around. The tagged event was the process, and the main bridi was at the named phase of that process. So mi klama le zarci pu'o le nu mi citka meant before my eating begins, I go to the store. You must reread text from the first edition accordingly. This includes the famous old example of this book, mi morsi ba'o le nu mi jmive, I am dead after living.

Contours used directly as tenses do not change. The sentence-connective forms also keep their meaning from the first edition. So ZAhO is the one tense whose subordinate and coordinate forms use the same sentence order (see ).

listitem.para: e-series attitudinalschange summary This change is editorial, and it follows usage. The senses taught here come from the language-definition committee's rework of these cmavo. The committee drafted and discussed that rework, but it never completed it or put it to a vote. Modern use attests the new senses, and the community's own contributions follow them. Coinages like e'ende (exhorts) and e'inde (instructs) show this.

In detail, .e'e is exhortation (in the first edition, competence), and .e'i is command (in the first edition, constraint). The opposite on the .e'o scale is now offer, and .ai nai is unintentionality, not refusal. The frozen official word lists keep the old senses, so expect them in older text (see ).

BAIchange summary This change is checkpointed (16 June 2005). The committee restated every BAI place by place, and it reversed the basic relation of no BAI. But the restatement was not empty. It filled in meanings for some thirty converted BAI, like te pi'o, that the tables of the first edition left blank. It also revised the place order of tai.

The restatement tightened several glosses to the checkpointed wording. The BAI ti'u is a time-of-day stamp. For ci'e, the se ci'e form became with system structure, not with system function, and ci'e gained a ve ci'e: with synergy in. The restatement also settled the old dispute about the reading of BAI plus -nai, in favor of this book (see ).
letteralschange summary This change is checkpointed (17 March 2004). The rule for the scope of shifts follows a later frozen decision of 11 February 2005. There are three changes.

First, a shift word applies only within its letteral string. In the first edition, a shift lasted in theory until a contradicting shift or the end of the text. But the first edition admitted that in practice, readers presumed that it expired at the first word that was not a letteral.
Second, the word .ybu counts as a unit before any word-level processing.

Third, a list of exceptions fixed the bu rules. The frozen list exempted the BAhE words and le'u, among others. In two corners, this edition follows the later synthesis instead. The list forbade ba'e bu and za'e bu, but the synthesis and current parsers permit them. The same is true of le'u bu.
See .

terminologychanges of, in this edition These changes are editorial. This edition makes three changes of terminology. It says group where the first edition said mass. It adopts the community term zi'evla for free-form borrowings. And it uses cmevla for the class of name words throughout.

section.title: Debated but not changed
section.para: Readers who know the community discussion can expect some changes that this edition deliberately does not make, because no official body ever adopted them:

listitem.para:
nascope of, unchanged A na before the selbri still negates the whole bridi. No official body adopted the proposal for a narrower scope in place. (But the positions of na relative to a tense now do differ. That is a de facto resolution: the semantic software that this edition surveyed implements it, and
teaches it.)

roexistential import, unchanged Restricted universal claims (ro da poi broda) still carry existential import, and this edition presents it as presuppositional. The alternative reading, with vacuous truth, never became settled. See .

distance tensesmedium readings, unchanged The middle members of the space and time series for distance and interval (va, za, ve'a, ze'a) keep their medium readings from the first edition. A regularization to unspecified circulated only as a proposal. So did a new reading of the tagged sumti of a distance word, as the distance itself and not as the reference point. See .
termsetsunchanged Termsets remain official. No official body adopted a proposal to eliminate them.

su'oinever adopted ro'oinever adopted To read the ratified, number-neutral lo as half of a formal system of plural logic is an unofficial analysis. No official body adopted the proposed plural quantifiers of that system, su'oi and ro'oi, and the standard grammar does not accept them. See .
lo'eunsettled status le'eunsettled status jeiunsettled status The words lo'e, le'e, and jei remain as unsettled as the first edition left them. This book marks them so where it teaches them.
